blind_spots: Limited non-English and enterprise-procurement perspective; segments skew toward indie/hobbyist vibe coders and US tech press.
CodeRabbit analysis quote is truncated in the evidence ('had 1.'), so the actual defect/severity finding is unknown.
Positive/success stories (e.g., shipping a game without coding, internal tooling wins) are present but underexplored as counter-signal context.
Evidence is heavily weighted toward Reddit, GitHub, and aggregator/blog summaries; little first-party telemetry or quantified productivity data beyond cited surveys.
Refusal-to-help behavior is referenced (Cursor telling a user to learn programming) but only as a headline with no clustered user-impact discussion in the rest of the evidence.
No evidence on latency/performance/speed of suggestions as a standalone pain point despite 'reliability over speed' framing.
contradictions: Productivity is framed both positively (AI builds internal tooling that 'would otherwise take weeks', a non-coder shipped a game in 8 months) and negatively (assistants 'slow you down, drain your credits' and one source titled 'AI coding assistants do not boost productivity').
Some users abandon tools because 'Copilot lies or produces bad results for a vast majority of the time' while others report substantial productivity benefits from the same class of tools.
Trust framing conflicts: declining trust (40%->29%, 46% distrust) coexists with continued heavy adoption and reliance reflected in volume of usage and tooling requests.
